title: Q&A: What is ‘long-duration energy storage’ – and why does the UK need it? - Carbon Brief
gist: The UK's long-duration energy storage (LDES) sector is scaling from 2.8GW of legacy pumped hydro toward a government-backed cap-and-floor mechanism that has provisionally awarded 7.6GW across 16 projects — dominated by pumped hydro and lithium-ion batteries concentrated in northern Scotland — with independent analysis putting the system-cost benefit at tens of billions of pounds through 2050.

insights.claim: The UK currently has just 2.8 gigawatts (GW) of long-duration energy storage, made up entirely of four legacy pumped-hydro sites in Scotland and Wales, the largest being the 1,728MW Dinorwig station opened in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The existing LDES base is tiny and technologically stagnant (no new pumped hydro since the 1980s), meaning almost all future UK LDES capacity growth must come from new technologies and new capital.
insights.locator: What is LDES?

insights.claim: There is no settled industry definition of LDES: the UK government (DESNZ) counts storage from 4 hours upward, Ofgem uses an 8-hour threshold, while some physicists argue true 'long duration' storage should mean seasons to decades, not hours (Sir Chris Llewellyn Smith, Royal Society/Oxford).
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Definitional inconsistency across UK policy bodies means capacity figures and targets quoted as 'LDES' are not directly comparable without checking the duration threshold used.
insights.quote: For us, long duration is stuff that can last not just into seasons, but into years and into decades.
insights.locator: What is LDES?

insights.claim: Lithium-ion batteries, traditionally a short-duration technology, are now routinely being built with 8-12 hours of storage, blurring the line with genuine long-duration storage (Ed Porter, Modo Energy).
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Lithium-ion's duration creep is displacing purpose-built long-duration technologies (flow batteries, compressed air, hydrogen) in near-term deployment, a competitive dynamic for LDES technology developers to watch.
insights.quote: Lithium [is] going far beyond 8 hours; that debate must surely be dead now.
insights.locator: Ed Porter, Modo Energy, on LinkedIn

insights.claim: Storage technologies fall into four broad categories — mechanical (pumped hydro, compressed air, liquid air, gravity), thermal, chemical (hydrogen salt-cavern) and electrochemical (lithium-ion, vanadium flow) — each with different duration and cost characteristics.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A working taxonomy for classifying LDES investment opportunities and matching technology type to system need (short peaks vs. seasonal storage).
insights.locator: What types of LDES are available?

insights.claim: Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen by an average of 20% per year over the past decade, the primary driver of their expansion into longer-duration use cases that were previously the domain of other technologies.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A 20%/year cost decline is a strong secular tailwind that continues to erode the cost advantage other LDES technologies (flow, compressed air, hydrogen) need to compete on.
insights.locator: What types of LDES are available?

insights.claim: Pumped hydro has the highest upfront capital cost of any LDES technology but a lifespan of over 50 years, giving it the lowest capital cost per kWh over time of any option — yet no new pumped-hydro project has been built in the UK since the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Pumped hydro's long-run economics remain the best of any LDES technology, but decades of non-deployment in the UK signal a project-development or planning bottleneck rather than a cost problem — worth watching as the cap-and-floor scheme now revives new pumped-hydro projects.
insights.locator: Pumped hydro is the most established LDES technology

insights.claim: LDES Council CEO Julia Souder argues the UK is pursuing a diverse LDES technology mix but expects only a handful of technologies to 'do the heavy lifting' over the next decade — a concentration already visible in the first cap-and-floor award round.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Investors backing niche LDES technologies (vanadium flow, compressed air, hydrogen) should expect these to remain a small minority of near-term deployed capacity relative to pumped hydro and lithium-ion.
insights.quote: a handful of LDES technologies will do the heavy lifting over the next decade
insights.locator: Julia Souder, LDES Council

insights.claim: The UK government's 2030 clean power action plan targets 4-6GW of LDES, alongside a much larger 23-27GW of short-duration battery storage, new interconnectors and consumer-led flexibility.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: LDES is a small slice of total UK 2030 storage targets compared with short-duration batteries — a useful benchmark for sizing the addressable LDES opportunity versus the broader battery storage market.
insights.locator: How much LDES will the UK need?

insights.claim: Neso's most recent Future Energy Scenarios project LDES climbing to between 13.2GW and 16.6GW by 2050, with the range driven mainly by how much hydrogen is used in the power system.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The long-run LDES capacity opportunity roughly triples from the 2030 target range, but the size of that opportunity hinges heavily on unresolved UK hydrogen-strategy decisions.
insights.locator: How much LDES will the UK need?

insights.claim: Neso warns that few LDES projects are likely to come online before 2030 given long development and planning timelines plus high capital expenditure requirements — a bottleneck risk to the clean-power-by-2030 target.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Even with a supportive cap-and-floor scheme in place, actual LDES capacity delivered by 2030 is likely to undershoot targets due to structural project-timeline constraints.
insights.locator: The Neso report notes that few LDES schemes

insights.claim: Of 171 LDES project applications (52.6GW total) submitted to Ofgem's cap-and-floor scheme in 2025, only 77 projects (28.7GW) passed to the assessment phase, and lithium-ion batteries dominated that pool with over 20GW of the roughly 29GW total.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Nearly two-thirds of applicant capacity was screened out before the assessment phase, and lithium-ion's dominance of what remained shows where near-term UK LDES capital is actually flowing.
insights.locator: Which types of LDES is the UK planning to use?

insights.claim: Ofgem is 'minded to' support 7.6GW of LDES across 16 projects, but only about 4GW is expected to be online by 2030 — the bottom end of the government's own 4-6GW target range for that year.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Even the first successful funding round only just meets the low end of the UK's own 2030 LDES target, implying limited headroom for the clean-power-2030 goal without further, faster project delivery.
insights.locator: Ultimately, Ofgem announced in June 2026

insights.claim: The successful 16-project shortlist spans just four technologies — pumped storage hydro (3.9GW), lithium batteries (3.6GW), one vanadium-zinc flow battery (65MW) and one compressed-air site (50MW) — while hydrogen, iron-air and sodium-sulphur batteries were shut out entirely.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The government's flagship LDES support mechanism is, in its first round, effectively a two-technology programme (pumped hydro and lithium) — a concentration risk and a signal of where near-term supplier and equipment demand will concentrate.

insights.claim: 79% of the shortlisted LDES capacity by storage volume is located in northern Scotland, reflecting where curtailed wind generation sits behind grid congestion (Ed Porter, Modo Energy).
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: LDES siting is following wind curtailment geography, meaning grid-connection and transmission bottlenecks in Scotland will remain the binding constraint even as storage capacity grows there.
insights.locator: Porter notes on LinkedIn

insights.claim: George Martin (LCP Delta) expects the total awarded LDES capacity to only rise, not fall, through Ofgem's ongoing consultation, though which specific projects make the final cut could still change.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The 7.6GW 'minded to' figure should be treated as a floor, not a ceiling, for the eventual final award — project-level composition remains the open variable to watch after the consultation closes.
insights.locator: George Martin, LCP Delta

insights.claim: LCP Delta's 2025 analysis finds that building 20GW of established medium-duration LDES (8-12 hour pumped hydro) by 2050 would deliver a system benefit of more than £10bn, while earlier 2023 analysis for DESNZ (by Regen and LCP Delta) put the benefit of the same 20GW at around £26bn.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Independent system-cost-benefit estimates for LDES vary several-fold depending on methodology and technology mix, so headline £bn savings figures for LDES should be read with their underlying assumptions in mind.
insights.locator: How could LDES impact energy bills?

insights.claim: The Transition Finance Council estimates LDES could cut total UK system costs by £7-13bn annually by 2040-2050, and that each gigawatt of long-duration flexibility requires roughly £2-2.5bn of investment but yields £0.5-1bn in annual system savings once operational — implying £30-60bn of net system savings over 25 years.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A per-GW payback framework (£2-2.5bn invested, £0.5-1bn annual return) gives investors a concrete unit-economics anchor for evaluating individual LDES project economics.
insights.locator: The Transition Finance Council report adds

insights.claim: In the 2024-25 financial year, UK system balancing costs reached £2.7bn (about £40 per household), of which £1.9bn (£28 per household) was tied specifically to wind curtailment — costs LDES is expected to reduce by absorbing surplus renewable output instead of paying generators to switch off.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Curtailment already costs UK households real money today; LDES capacity growth has a direct, quantifiable near-term bill-reduction pathway rather than only a long-run theoretical benefit.
insights.locator: In the financial year 2024-25, balancing costs reached £2.7bn

insights.claim: LDES lets the system use the existing renewable fleet more efficiently by storing surplus wind and solar and displacing gas generation during high-demand periods, cutting both emissions and system costs (George Martin, LCP Delta).
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: LDES buildout is a substitute for gas-fired peaking capacity, meaning its growth should be watched as a headwind to gas-plant utilisation and revenue in a renewables-heavy UK grid.
insights.locator: Martin says LDES will allow the UK to 'use our renewable fleet more efficiently'

insights.claim: Seamus Garvey (University of Nottingham) warns that current heavy investment in short-duration batteries is crowding out the market space and revenue streams that longer-duration storage projects need to attract financing, worsening an already difficult LDES financing problem.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Short-duration battery growth may be a structural headwind, not just a competitor, to longer-duration technologies' ability to raise financing — a risk factor for LDES project developers and their lenders.
insights.quote: we are actually removing pieces of market that could be accessible by longer duration stores and that is making the (already-difficult) problem of financing these stores ever more difficult
insights.locator: Seamus Garvey, University of Nottingham

insights.claim: Innovate UK is putting up to £10m (with £3m in an initial phase) behind 'ultra-long' duration battery storage capable of at least 100 continuous discharge hours, signalling government interest in pushing beyond the lithium-ion and pumped-hydro technologies that dominated the first cap-and-floor round.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A dedicated public funding stream for 100+ hour storage points to where UK policy is trying to seed a next-generation LDES technology cohort beyond today's cap-and-floor winners.
